payload.roles:
INHERITS the first pass's nine (walking agent, arriving agent, owner-as-adjudicator, owner-as-auditor, owner-as-operator, the retro, the future iteration, the engine itself, external tool maintainers).

ONE ROLE IS ADDED, and its absence from the first pass is the clearest single explanation of what went wrong:

THE REVIEWER - whoever reads the work against its claims before a gate is blessed. In v1 this was the OWNER by default, and the contract said so: the agent never self-certifies a killer. In v2 the role still EXISTS in the method (meth-gate-review assigns it four rounds) but is assigned to NOBODY - the delegation moved it to the agent that did the work, and no artifact ever asked that agent to perform it. A role with a job, no holder, and no prompt is a role that does not act. Naming it as a role rather than as a step is the point: it makes the vacancy visible, and the vacancy is what this iteration is filling with the least-bad available holder.
payload.tensions:
INHERITS T1-T6 (guidance volume, speed vs traceability, adjudicator vs auditor, operator vs no-fallback, the engine vs everyone, the retro under-served).

T4 IS RESOLVED rather than carried: the operator-versus-no-fallback tension was created by dropping ripgrep. With the owner's correction restoring two tools for two jobs, ripgrep returns WITH its own risk entry, and the tension reverts to the ordinary accepted-dependency shape.

THREE TENSIONS ARE ADDED, all created by the new REVIEWER role.

T7 THE REVIEWER vs THE WALKING AGENT - THEY ARE THE SAME ENTITY. This is not a tension between parties; it is a tension inside one, which is worse because nothing external resolves it. The walking agent wants its work to pass; the reviewer's job is to find why it should not. RULED, and honestly: the kill-criterion is the only real defence - naming in advance what would make the decision wrong is a commitment made BEFORE you know whether you will find it. It does not make the agent want to find it. Logged as se.raid-mandatory-rounds-degrade-into-ceremony; the structural answer is a separate party and it is out of scope.

T8 THE REVIEWER vs THE OWNER'S AUTONOMY GOAL. v1 resolved T7 by making the reviewer a human. That resolution is unavailable: the owner has ruled that the involvement slider must reach zero and that the fix for quality is mechanical, never more human review. So v2 must keep the reviewer role filled by the agent and make the ROUNDS carry the weight the human used to carry. RULED: accept the weaker holder, make the round's FORM as demanding as possible (kill-criterion named, what was found reported, override logged with dissent), and measure ceremony at the retro rather than assuming sincerity.

T9 THE REVIEWER vs THE FUTURE ITERATION. Four mandatory rounds on every gate is a permanent tax on every iteration forever, and most gates are not close calls. RULED from v1's rubric rather than invented: SCALE TO SIZE - do not red-team a trivial gate - but SAY SO in the round. 'This gate is mechanical, no opposing case exists' is a review; an empty field is not. The cost is then proportional to the risk rather than flat.

AND ONE NON-TENSION WORTH RECORDING: I looked for a conflict between the reviewer and the RETRO and found none - they want the same thing, which is why the retro is where ceremony gets detected. The first pass noted that a design nobody objects to usually hides a missing role. This time the missing role was found.
